name: messaging-mapper
intent: Keep domain objects and the messaging infrastructure independent by giving the conversion between them a component of its own - a Messaging Mapper that builds a message from domain objects on the way out and creates or updates domain objects from incoming messages on the way in, while neither side knows the mapper exists.
problem: An application that exchanges messages has domain objects shaped for behaviour (object references, invariants, lazy associations, inheritance) and messages shaped for transport (a flat serialisable body plus headers). If every producer copies fields into a payload and every consumer parses fields back, the conversion is duplicated at every endpoint, the domain learns the wire format, the message contract learns domain internals, and a change on either side ripples through all the call sites. The recurring decision is not whether to convert - it must be converted - but where the conversion lives and which side, if either, is allowed to know about it.
context: Application-to-application messaging at a boundary where both sides deserve to survive independently: the domain model owns invariants and object references that the wire cannot carry, the message contract is a published interface other applications consume, and the messaging technology (JMS, AMQP/Service Bus, Kafka, a queue library) should be replaceable without touching domain code. It applies at message endpoints and channel adapters - command and event producers, document-message consumers, request/reply services and batch channels - and remains valid when the mapper is generated or declared instead of hand-written.
benefits: Both sides stay clean: the domain keeps object references, invariants and behaviour, the message keeps a flat serialisable versioned body, and neither type imports the other's types.

One home for every conversion rule - which objects contribute, reference flattening, units, time stamps, absent-versus-default and what is deliberately dropped - instead of field copying repeated at each endpoint.

The message contract becomes an explicit interface: shape and compatibility policy (what may be added, what a missing field means) are reviewable and versionable rather than implied by whichever code happened to copy fields.
The mapper is a pure, dependency-light unit, so boundary behaviour is tested with golden messages and round trips instead of only through a broker.
Transport independence: switching broker, serialisation format or channel topology changes the endpoint and the encoder, not the mapping rules and not the domain.
Deliberate exposure: because the mapper names exactly what crosses, fields that are not translated cannot leak - useful for data minimisation, redaction and stable public payloads.
tradeoffs: A third artefact per message pair and permanent maintenance: every field added, renamed or re-typed on either side is a mapper change, and hand-written field copying is repetitive by nature.
Drift is silent: little ties the two shapes together, so a forgotten field ships as a null or a zero and is usually noticed downstream, not at the mapper.

Flattening is lossy by construction: object references, polymorphism and identity become ids and discriminators, and the inbound direction must decide how to re-resolve or create objects - a decision that easily leaks domain rules into the mapper.

Copy and encode costs per message: building a message from an aggregate and serialising it duplicates allocation, CPU and payload size on hot paths, and an eagerly mapped aggregate bloats the message with data the consumer never reads.
The mapper attracts what does not belong to it: validation, defaulting, authorisation and business rules creep in until it is a shadow domain layer with no owner and no invariants of its own.

Version burden: the message is a public contract, so every mapped field is a compatibility commitment; producers and consumers deployed at different times force explicit tolerance rules (ignore unknown fields, fail on missing required ones) that only the mapper can own.

participants.responsibility: Owns both directions and every conversion rule between the domain objects and the message: which objects contribute, how references flatten to ids, units, time stamps, absent-versus-default and what is dropped. Contains no I/O and no business rules.
The business model the message is derived from, or that is created/updated from a message. Carries its own invariants and references and knows nothing about messages, channels or the mapper.
The transport artefact - a flat serialisable body plus headers - that the mapper produces or consumes. Knows nothing about domain objects, their identity or their relationships.
Invokes the mapper at the right moment: the producer maps before sending, the consumer maps before handing the result to domain code. Owns the channel and the wire encoding, never the mapping rules.

use_cases: Event publication: an application service completes a transaction and sends a domain event; the mapper builds the event message from the aggregate (identity, flattened references, timestamps, the fields consumers may see) while the aggregate stays persistence-shaped.

Command consumption at the edge: a queue carries a command message; the endpoint invokes the inbound direction to load or create the aggregate, resolve referenced entities and apply the change, keeping the messaging API out of the domain.

One public contract, several consumers: the same aggregate is published as one canonical message shape to partners, while internal consumers receive a smaller projection produced by a second mapper from the same object.

Anti-corruption at an integration seam: a partner's flat payload is mapped into the local model by one mapper hosted in the adapter, so neither the partner's schema nor its conventions reach the domain.

Request/reply services: a service endpoint maps an incoming request message to domain arguments and the result or error back to a reply message, with correlation decided in the mapper rather than in domain code.

Contract testing and migrations: the mapper is the single place where payload versions are recognised, so v1/v2 compatibility and consumer-driven contract tests target one unit instead of every producer and consumer.

Apache Camel Messaging Mapper EIP: a route can keep domain objects separate while a mapper or type converter turns them into the message body or back, with Camel's conversion registry and wire transport remaining outside the domain.

WSO2 Micro Integrator: Message Builders and Message Formatters provide the serialization/deserialization seam for XML/SOAP and JSON, allowing protocol-specific representation to remain outside domain-facing objects.

Spring AMQP and MassTransit: Spring's MessageConverter handles object-to-message and message-to-object conversion using message metadata, while MassTransit keeps message contracts as plain data types; both illustrate a dedicated contract boundary instead of exposing persistence entities.
avoid_when: The domain type already is the message: a plain serialisable record with no references, no lazy state and no invariants beyond its fields - serialise it directly and skip the layer.
The message differs from the object by one field or one name: an inline conversion at that single call site is honest and cheaper than a mapper.
Both sides are messages (a wire-format change or a mapping between two payload shapes): that is Message Translator's job, not a domain-object mapper.
The conversion is really business logic - pricing, eligibility, invariant repair: it belongs in the domain or a domain service, not in a boundary mapper.

The framework already owns the mapping declaratively and adequately (schema-first IDL code generation, serializer attributes on a dedicated contract type, ORM-style generated mappers): declare fields there instead of writing a second mapper by hand.
anti_patterns: Domain-owned mapping: to_message()/from_message() methods or serialisation hooks on the aggregate put the wire contract inside the domain, so every model change touches messaging code - the pattern inverted.

Entity as message: reusing the persistence entity (with its ORM annotations and navigation properties) as the payload, so the message contract changes with the database schema and a lazy association can be serialised or trigger a query.
Endpoint copying: each producer and consumer copies fields itself, so the conversion exists in N places, disagrees about absent values and can be reviewed and tested only per call site.

Whole-object dump: serialising the aggregate graph straight into the body - every field, internal flag and collection - which accidentally publishes domain internals and grows the payload without bound.

Mapper as shadow domain: validation, defaults and business rules accumulate in the mapper, invariants end up outside the model, and the mapper path and any other entry point treat the same data differently.

Symmetric round trip assumed: the inbound direction pretends to rebuild exactly the object the outbound direction saw, ignoring identity, references and aggregate boundaries, so load-modify-store over messaging is not idempotent.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: translation between representations is its own responsibility, distinct from domain behaviour and from transport mechanics.
Single responsibility: one mapper per domain-type/message-type pair, named for both sides, with both directions in the same place.
Dependency inversion with dependencies pointing inward: the domain depends on nothing, the mapper lives in the outer layer and depends on both representations.
Information hiding: only the mapper knows both representations; what is not deliberately translated does not cross the boundary.
Explicit contract: the message is a published interface whose shape and compatibility policy are reviewable, versioned and testable.
Single direction of knowledge: the mapper knows the domain object and the message; neither knows the mapper.
best_practices: Give every pair exactly one mapper with both directions as named operations (to_message/from_message) and let no other code copy fields across that boundary.
Keep the mapper pure: no network, database, file or clock access; pass identity resolution and time in as arguments so the mapping stays a function of its inputs.
Make the absent-versus-default policy explicit per field and per direction (fail, default, ignore, quarantine) instead of letting a missing value become a plausible zero.
Flatten deliberately: replace references with stable ids, decide what is inlined, and document what was dropped so the message contract states its own coverage.
Let the endpoint and the serialisation library own the wire encoding; the mapper produces or consumes a message value and never writes to the channel itself.
Table-test the mapper with golden messages and round trips, including unknown fields, unknown enum values, units and version skew - mapper bugs are silent by nature.
Keep the message contract a dedicated type: no domain types, no ORM annotations and no behaviour beyond the boundary invariants the channel requires.
Version the contract like an API and make the inbound direction tolerant of additions (ignore or quarantine unknown fields) while failing loudly on missing required data.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Messaging Mapper (Messaging Endpoints chapter): create a separate mapper that contains the mapping logic between the messaging infrastructure and the domain objects, so that neither the objects nor the infrastructure know of its existence.
Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003) - Mapper (Base Patterns, ch. 18) and Data Mapper (ch. 10): the EIP catalog describes Messaging Mapper as a specialization of Mapper.
